notes: NON-DISCRIMINATING BENCHMARK: all 22 assertions pass in both configurations (100% vs 100%, delta +0.00). Opus 5 at max effort already splits, orders and messages commits competently without the skill, so these assertions measure floor behaviour the model clears unaided. They validate the skill does no harm; they do not measure its value.

The real differences are qualitative and live in message CONTENT, not commit structure. Commit grouping was identical across configurations in all three evals (3 / 2 / 1 commits, same file groupings).

eval-0 (mixed-concerns): with_skill bodies open with the status quo before describing the change — the article's 'Context' question. The export commit body starts "`tracker list` is the only way to get entries out, and it prints a human-readable table that is awkward to load into a spreadsheet". The baseline's body for the same commit is implementation-only: "Adds internal/export.CSV, which writes entries as comma separated values..." — it restates the diff without saying why.

eval-2 (single-change): both runs silently discovered the same latent defect (the appended test called convertAll but the file's require() did not import it) and both fixed it. with_skill documented the fix in the commit body; the baseline shipped a subject-only message, leaving an unrelated-looking edit unexplained for a reviewer.

POSSIBLE REGRESSION — eval-1: with_skill capitalised its subjects ("Raise default timeout from 30s to 120s") while the baseline stayed lowercase ("raise default timeout from 30s to 120s"). That fixture's history is lowercase. The skill's worked example is capitalised (the article's "Add '--gray' option alias"), which may be overriding the 'match house style' instruction given earlier in the skill.

COST: with_skill is meaningfully slower and more expensive for no assertion gain — 121.3s vs 91.4s mean (+33%) and 29,336 vs 25,040 tokens (+17%). The extra spend buys richer message bodies; whether that trade is worth it is the user's call.

EVAL DEFECT to fix before iteration 2: the eval-2 fixture shipped a broken test import, so both runs spent effort on an incidental repair unrelated to what the eval was testing (over-splitting and house style).
